value.overview: The White-throated Magpie-Jay (Cyanocorax formosus) is a large, conspicuous corvid of dry forests and open woodland in western Central America. It is recognized by its long blue-and-white tail, bold black-and-white head pattern, and prominent forward-curving crest. These intelligent, noisy birds commonly travel in groups and use a wide range of natural and modified habitats. In Costa Rica, the species is most characteristic of the dry Pacific northwest.
value.classification: It belongs to the family Corvidae, which includes crows, ravens, jays, and magpies. The species has also traditionally been placed in the genus Calocitta, and some field guides still use the name Calocitta formosa.
value.identification: A White-throated Magpie-Jay has rich blue upperparts, a very long blue-and-white tail, a black face and upper breast, and a broad white throat and lower breast. Its most distinctive feature is the tall, swept-forward crest, which is usually blue, black, and white. The sexes are similar, although females are generally duller, with a shorter tail and a less prominent chest band. Its loud, varied calls and active behavior make it easy to notice.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges along the Pacific side of Mexico and Central America, from western Mexico south through Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and into Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is primarily associated with the dry northwest, especially Guanacaste and adjacent northern Puntarenas, where it occurs in tropical dry forest, thorn scrub, woodland edges, pastures with scattered trees, plantations, and other open or semi-open habitats. It is generally found from lowlands into lower foothills.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident and non-migratory. In Costa Rica, White-throated Magpie-Jays remain year-round in suitable Pacific-slope habitats, although local movements may follow food availability and seasonal rainfall.
value.breeding: White-throated Magpie-Jays breed in wooded savanna, dry forest, scrub, and forest-edge settings. Nests are usually placed in trees, sometimes in relatively isolated trees standing in clearings or pasture. The species is socially complex and may breed in groups, with other birds helping defend territories or assist around the nest. Breeding activity is linked to the local rainy season and food conditions, but the exact timing can vary across its range. Several pale eggs are laid in a stick nest.
value.dietFeeding: The diet is varied and includes fruits, seeds, insects, other invertebrates, and small vertebrates or eggs when available. These jays forage in trees, shrubs, and on the ground, searching actively with their bills and feet. In Costa Rica’s dry forests, fruits and seeds are especially important during seasonal changes in food supply. They also readily exploit cultivated areas, garden food, and opportunities around human settlements.
value.behavior: This is a highly social, vocal, and conspicuous jay. Groups move through vegetation while giving harsh calls, whistles, rattles, and other notes, and they may mob predators or intruders. White-throated Magpie-Jays are agile climbers and strong fliers but often spend time walking or hopping on the ground. Their intelligence, curiosity, and tolerance of open habitats allow them to live near farms, roads, villages, and tourist areas.

conservation.populationTrend: No reliable evidence of a significant global decline is established for the species.
